title: "Chapter 2 In-Class R Demo: Mean, Variance, and ACF"

## Demo Goal

You will see why time-series data need covariance and autocorrelation, not only mean and variance.

Reference anchor: stationarity, autocovariance, and sample ACF ideas from the reference texts.

```{r setup}
set.seed(311)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 1. Two Series with Similar Mean and Variance

```{r compare-series}
n <- 200
white_noise <- rnorm(n)

ar_series <- numeric(n)
phi <- 0.8
eps <- rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - phi^2))  # Var(X_t) = 1, like the noise
for (t in 2:n) {
  ar_series[t] <- phi * ar_series[t - 1] + eps[t]
}

mean(white_noise)
var(white_noise)
mean(ar_series)
var(ar_series)
```

```{r compare-plots}
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot.ts(white_noise, main = "White noise", ylab = "X_t")
plot.ts(ar_series, main = "Autocorrelated series", ylab = "X_t")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Questions:

- If the mean and variance are not enough, what extra feature do we need?

## 2. ACF as a Picture of Memory

```{r acf-comparison}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(white_noise, main = "ACF: white noise")
acf(ar_series, main = "ACF: autocorrelated")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Questions:

- Which series remembers its past?
- How does the ACF show this?

## 3. Manual Autocovariance

```{r manual-acvf}
sample_autocov <- function(x, h) {
  xbar <- mean(x)
  n <- length(x)
  sum((x[(h + 1):n] - xbar) * (x[1:(n - h)] - xbar)) / n
}

gamma0 <- sample_autocov(ar_series, 0)
gamma1 <- sample_autocov(ar_series, 1)
rho1 <- gamma1 / gamma0

c(gamma0 = gamma0, gamma1 = gamma1, rho1 = rho1)
acf(ar_series, plot = FALSE)$acf[1:3]
```

Try it yourself:

- Change `phi <- 0.8` to `phi <- -0.8`.
- Rerun the plots and ACF.
- Why does the series now alternate?

## 4. ACF by Hand with Five Observations

Start with a small series, so you can check every number by hand.

```{r acf-by-hand-small}
x_small <- c(4, 5, 6, 5, 4)
xbar <- mean(x_small)
deviation <- x_small - xbar

data.frame(
  t = seq_along(x_small),
  x = x_small,
  deviation = deviation
)
```

The lag 0 autocovariance is the average squared deviation.

```{r gamma0-small}
gamma0_parts <- deviation * deviation
gamma0 <- sum(gamma0_parts) / length(x_small)

data.frame(part = gamma0_parts)
gamma0
```

The lag 1 autocovariance compares each deviation with the previous deviation.

```{r gamma1-small}
lag1_parts <- deviation[2:5] * deviation[1:4]
gamma1 <- sum(lag1_parts) / length(x_small)
rho1 <- gamma1 / gamma0

data.frame(
  current_deviation = deviation[2:5],
  previous_deviation = deviation[1:4],
  product = lag1_parts
)
c(gamma1 = gamma1, rho1 = rho1)
```

The lag 2 autocovariance compares observations two periods apart.

```{r gamma2-small}
lag2_parts <- deviation[3:5] * deviation[1:3]
gamma2 <- sum(lag2_parts) / length(x_small)
rho2 <- gamma2 / gamma0

data.frame(
  current_deviation = deviation[3:5],
  lag2_deviation = deviation[1:3],
  product = lag2_parts
)
c(gamma2 = gamma2, rho2 = rho2)
```

Compare the hand calculation with R's built-in ACF.

```{r compare-hand-to-r}
acf(x_small, plot = FALSE)$acf[1:3]
```

Questions:

- What does a positive product mean?
- What does a negative product mean?
- Why can lag 2 be negative even when lag 1 is near zero?

## 5. Predict the ACF Before Plotting

```{r predict-acf-activity}
upward <- c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
zigzag <- c(2, 6, 2, 6, 2)
flat <- c(3, 3, 3, 3, 3)

acf_by_hand <- function(x, max_lag = 4) {
  xbar <- mean(x)
  dev <- x - xbar
  gamma0 <- sum(dev * dev) / length(x)
  out <- data.frame(lag = 0:max_lag, gamma = NA_real_, rho = NA_real_)
  for (h in 0:max_lag) {
    products <- dev[(h + 1):length(x)] * dev[1:(length(x) - h)]
    out$gamma[h + 1] <- sum(products) / length(x)
    out$rho[h + 1] <- out$gamma[h + 1] / gamma0
  }
  out
}

acf_by_hand(upward)
acf_by_hand(zigzag)
```

For `flat`, the ACF is not meaningful because there is no variation.

```{r flat-case}
var(flat)
```

## 6. Covariance and Correlation: Air Quality in New York

The notes use the 26 complete days of May 1973 from the built-in `airquality`
data. Here we use all complete days, May to September 1973 (ozone in ppb,
solar radiation, wind speed in mph, temperature in degrees F).

```{r air}
air <- na.omit(airquality[, c("Ozone", "Solar.R", "Wind", "Temp")])
head(air)
summary(air)
dim(air)
```

```{r air-scatter}
plot(air$Wind, air$Ozone, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Wind speed (mph)", ylab = "Ozone (ppb)",
     main = "New York, May-September 1973: ozone vs wind")
fit_a <- lm(Ozone ~ Wind, data = air)
abline(fit_a, col = "grey40", lwd = 2)
coef(fit_a)
summary(fit_a)$r.squared
```

`cov()` and `cor()` use the divisor n - 1. Check them by hand.

```{r air-cov}
n <- nrow(air)
dev_oz <- air$Ozone - mean(air$Ozone)
dev_wd <- air$Wind - mean(air$Wind)

c(cov_R = cov(air$Ozone, air$Wind),
  cov_hand = sum(dev_oz * dev_wd) / (n - 1))
c(cor_R = cor(air$Ozone, air$Wind),
  cor_hand = sum(dev_oz * dev_wd) / sqrt(sum(dev_oz^2) * sum(dev_wd^2)))

round(cor(air), 2)
pairs(air, main = "Air quality: scatterplot matrix")
```

Questions:

- Is the linear association between ozone and wind strong or weak? Which
  points drive it? Compare with the May-only value in the notes.
- Why is the squared correlation equal to the R-squared of the fitted line?
- Do the divisors n and n - 1 change the correlation? Why not?
- The observations are consecutive days. Why might that matter when we judge
  whether a correlation is "significant" (Chapter 2, Section 2.4)?

## 7. Lag Scatterplots and the ACF: Wave Heights

The simulated wave heights of the wave-height example in the notes (396
readings in mm).
A lag-k scatterplot plots each value against the value k steps later.

```{r wave}
set.seed(311)
wave <- round(arima.sim(model = list(ar = c(0.8, -0.6)), n = 396, sd = 200))
summary(as.numeric(wave))
plot(wave, main = "Wave heights (simulated)",
     xlab = "Time", ylab = "Wave height (mm)")
```

```{r wave-lags, fig.height = 4.5}
n <- length(wave)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(wave[1:(n - 1)], wave[2:n], pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Lag 1", xlab = expression(x[t]), ylab = expression(x[t + 1]))
fit_lag1 <- lm(wave[2:n] ~ wave[1:(n - 1)])
abline(fit_lag1, col = "grey40", lwd = 2)
plot(wave[1:(n - 3)], wave[4:n], pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Lag 3", xlab = expression(x[t]), ylab = expression(x[t + 3]))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

coef(fit_lag1)[2]                    # slope of the lag-1 line
acf(wave, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]       # sample ACF at lag 1
```

```{r wave-acf}
acf_wave <- acf(wave, main = "Sample ACF of the wave heights")
round(acf_wave$acf[2:11], 3)         # lags 1 to 10

rho1 <- acf_wave$acf[2]
bound <- 1.96 / sqrt(length(wave))
cat(sprintf("Lag-1 ACF: %.3f; 95%% bounds: +/-%.4f; the value lies %s.\n",
            rho1, bound, if (abs(rho1) > bound) "outside" else "inside"))
```

Questions:

- Why is the slope of the lag-1 line close to the lag-1 sample ACF?
- What does the lag-3 scatterplot show, and how does it match the ACF at lag 3?
- How many lags fall outside the bounds? Would you expect any for iid white noise?

Try it yourself:

- Run `lag.plot(wave, lags = 4)` to see lags 1 to 4 at once.
- Replace `wave` by `LakeHuron` or `lh` and compare the lag plots and ACF.

## 8. The ACF of Nonstationary Series

A random walk $X_t = X_{t-1} + \epsilon_t$ and the `AirPassengers` series of
the notes. The sample ACF can be computed for any data, but here it does not
estimate the ACF of a stationary process.

```{r nonstationary-acf, fig.height = 7}
rw <- cumsum(rnorm(200))               # random walk with X_0 = 0
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot.ts(rw, main = "Random walk", ylab = "X_t")
acf(rw, lag.max = 40, main = "ACF: random walk")
plot(AirPassengers, main = "AirPassengers", ylab = "Passengers (1000s)")
acf(as.numeric(AirPassengers), lag.max = 40, main = "ACF: AirPassengers",
    xlab = "Lag (months)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Questions:

- Why does the random-walk sample ACF start near 1 and decay almost linearly,
  although $\text{E}(X_t) = 0$ for every $t$?
- At which lags does the `AirPassengers` ACF have local peaks, and why?

Try it yourself:

- Run `acf(diff(rw))`. What do the differences look like?
